canonicalExplanation.summary: Without constraints, a template error appears **deep inside** the template, pages away from the real mistake. **Concepts** state requirements at the **boundary**: `template <std::random_access_iterator It>` or `requires std::sortable<It>`. If a call doesn't satisfy them, the error names the **unsatisfied requirement at your call site**, and overload resolution can simply skip that template. A `requires` expression lists operations that must **compile**, for example `requires (T a) { a.size(); }`. It's checked at compile time and **never runs** anything. Concepts check syntax plus the documented meaning: they can't prove your algorithm works for every value.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner writes a sort_all helper and calls it with a std::list. The compiler prints 90 lines about iterator subtraction inside std::sort. With a constrained version, the error is one line at the call: the list's iterator isn't random access. A sorting helper requires random-access iteration and sortable values, rejecting a list iterator at the call boundary. In this lesson you'll explain why an instantiation fails and improve its requirement or call site.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Standard algorithms**, **Class interface and invariants**, **Function templates** and **Warnings and diagnostics** (reading candidate notes).

sections.heading: The rule: state requirements at the boundary
Fixing the call or the requirement

includes: Read constraint failures and decide whether to fix the call site or the requirement.
Write concepts and requires expressions that state the operations a template uses.
excludes: Subsumption and concept ordering in depth.

outcomes: Explain why an instantiation fails and improve its requirement or call site.

examples.title: Sorting a std::list by mistake
examples.situation: A sorting helper requires random-access iteration and sortable values, rejecting a list iterator at the call boundary.
walkthrough: **A sorting helper requires random-access iteration and sortable values:** template <std::random_access_iterator It> requires std::sortable<It>.
**Rejecting a list iterator:** sort_all(l.begin(), l.end()) fails because list iterators are bidirectional.
**At the call boundary:** the one-line error points at main; the fix will be l.sort().
examples.result: The error explains itself, and the learner picks the right tool.

examples.title: The over-strict requirement
examples.situation: A print_all template requires std::random_access_range, so it rejects std::list and std::set even though it only loops over elements.
walkthrough: The body only uses a range-for.
examples.result: The constraint matches what the template really uses.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A requires expression executes sample operations at runtime and proves the algorithm will succeed for every value.
misconceptions.correction: Requires expressions are compile-time checks that operations are valid. They don't run code or prove run-time correctness; tests do that.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, when is a requires expression checked?

analogy.example: A concept is like **the height sign at a roller coaster entrance**. It stops unsuitable riders **at the gate** (call site) instead of halfway through the ride (deep in the template). But it doesn't guarantee a good ride: that still needs safety checks (tests).
usefulFor: the sign isn't a safety test
limitations: Height is easy to measure; semantics aren't.
An over-strict sign turns away riders who'd be fine.

steps.explanation: The sorting helper requires random-access iteration and sortable values.
A list iterator is rejected at the call boundary.
The call site switches to an algorithm the list supports.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing a constraint failure. Step 1, Accept: It is vector iterator; constraint is satisfied. The sorting helper requires random-access iteration and sortable values. Step 2, Reject: It is list iterator; error is random_access_iterator not satisfied. A list iterator is rejected at the call boundary. Step 3, Fix: call is l.sort(); result is 1 2 3. The call site switches to an algorithm the list supports.

nearTransfer.prompt: Write a concept Printable<T> requiring std::cout << t to compile, constrain a print function with it, and call it with int, std::string and a struct without operator<<. Read the error.
scaffold: requires (std::ostream& os, const T& t) { os << t; }.

farTransfer.prompt: Take an unconstrained template that fails deep inside for some types. Identify every operation it uses, write a concept for exactly those, and compare the error messages before and after for a bad call.
expectedEvidence: Short error at the call site.

remediation.explanation: When a constraint fails, read **which requirement** is unsatisfied, then ask: **is my argument wrong for this template, or is the requirement stricter than the body needs?**

recap.summary: To explain and fix constraint failures, state a template's requirements with concepts or requires clauses at its boundary, read which requirement a call fails, then either change the call site to a suitable type or algorithm or relax the requirement to what the body truly uses, remembering concepts are compile-time checks, not proofs of behaviour.
